book.title: The Telegraph All New Toughie Crossword, book 1

clue.text: t~ Crowd spiteful? One may have got this from the paper

definitions.text: One may have got this from the paper

parts.note: stray marks from the scanned page, not part of the clue
to crowd is to press, and a crowd is a press of people
a cutting remark is a spiteful one

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a crowd is being spiteful, then muses that a person might have picked up the idea from a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is a description rather than a synonym: a clipping saved from a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A press cutting is an article clipped out of a newspaper, so it is something a reader gets from the paper.

clue.text: Turn up to participate in helping with Christian observance

indicators.note: in places those letters inside the following word

parts.note: a ration is a helping or portion

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning words up means writing them from bottom to top, in reverse order

parts.note: to have a go is to take part

explanation.surface: Arrive to join in assisting at a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn up' looks like 'arrive', but it reverses the word for participate, which then goes inside the portion.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogation days are Christian days of prayer and fasting before Ascension, so the word names a church observance.

clue.text: Strip of cloth cut, short length removed

indicators.note: removed means taken away, so that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: to slash is to cut
L is the short form of length

explanation.surface: A strip of fabric has been trimmed, a little of its length taken off.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a long band of cloth worn around the waist or over a shoulder.

clue.text: It's to do with bothering

definitions.meaning: first meaning: about, regarding, a preposition
second meaning: worrying or troubling, as an adjective

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one statement about bother, but splits into a preposition and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means regarding as a preposition, and worrying or troubling as an adjective.

clue.text: Hard gold in the Government's money chest

indicators.note: in places those letters inside the following word

parts.note: what the government takes is tax
H for hard, as on pencils
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Solid gold is kept in the state's treasury strongbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money chest' reads as one strongbox, but 'chest' alone is the definition and 'the Government's money' gives the tax.
explanation.definitionFit: The thorax is the part of the body between neck and abdomen, the chest.

clue.text: I'm Uri and I'd buckle metal

indicators.note: to buckle is to bend out of shape, so these letters are distorted into a new order

parts.note: the letters of I'm, Uri and I'd, with 'and' only joining them

explanation.surface: Uri Geller, the spoon-bending showman, boasts he would bend metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Iridium is a hard, dense metallic element of the platinum group.

clue.text: Potter's so-called skill made to look silly by a misshapen hollow mug

indicators.note: letters made to look silly are put into a ridiculous arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: something hollow has had its insides scooped out, leaving only its outer shell

parts.note: just the first and last letters of mug

explanation.surface: A potter's craft is mocked by a badly formed, empty mug.
explanation.walkthrough: The potter is not a ceramicist but Stephen Potter, the British humorist who wrote 'The Theory and Practice of Gamesmanship'; 'misshapen' looks like an anagram signal but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Potter coined the term for winning games through dubious psychological ploys without actually cheating.

clue.text: Athlete's garment

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a competitor in a high or long jump event
second meaning: a knitted pullover, the British word for a sweater

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one sportsman's kit, but the possessive only joins two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an athlete who jumps, and in Britain a pullover sweater.

clue.text: Old walled town supplying half the wine

indicators.note: taking half of a word means keeping only its first four of eight letters and dropping the rest

parts.note: the wine from eastern France named after its region

explanation.surface: An ancient fortified town is said to produce half of a famous wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The wine' is not a general word for wine but one particular wine, whose first half is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A burg is an old term for a fortified town or borough, hence an old walled town.

clue.text: Simon sure turns out to be a bit of a brain

indicators.note: something that turns out differently ends up in an altered form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the two words are taken letter for letter as raw material

explanation.surface: A man called Simon is confident he will prove to be a bit of a brainbox.
explanation.definitionFit: The sensorium is the part of the brain that receives and interprets sensations, so it is one portion of a brain.

clue.text: Unimportant people who get involved in fights?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: people of little influence or substance
second meaning: boxers of a particular weight division, hinted by the question mark

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads like brawlers, but it points at a boxing weight class.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is used both for insignificant people and for boxers in a weight division between featherweight and welterweight.

clue.text: One unable to speak, keeping quiet, bringing credit

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a thing keeping something holds it within, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: someone who cannot speak is mute
p, piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot talk keeps silent and so earns praise.
explanation.walkthrough: The quiet sign sits inside the word for speechless, after the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: To impute something to someone is to credit or attribute it to them, as in crediting a deed to its doer.

clue.text: Coin showing Persian king with Eastern name inscribed

indicators.note: writing inscribed on a coin is set into its surface, so these letters are set inside another word

parts.note: Darius was the name of several kings of ancient Persia
E is the abbreviation for Eastern
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A coin bears the head of a Persian king with an oriental name engraved on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The two abbreviations go in after the king's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The denarius was the standard silver coin of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Old Greek bridges spanning one huge stretch of water

indicators.note: a bridge spanning something stretches across it from side to side, so the outer word encloses the rest

parts.note: arches are spans, as of a bridge
the Roman numeral for one
the Med, short for the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: Ancient Greek bridges cross a vast sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The numeral and the sea go inside the word for bridges, after its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes was a mathematician and inventor of ancient Syracuse in the Greek world.

clue.text: Protecting various characters from rough Brian

indicators.note: various characters taken from a phrase means its letters used in a different arrangement

parts.note: both words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: Assorted people are being shielded from a thuggish man called Brian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' reads as a description of Brian, but it supplies half the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Harbouring someone means sheltering or giving refuge to them, a way of protecting them.

clue.text: Girl providing mathematical premise, learner breaking out

indicators.note: one breaking out of a place escapes and is no longer in it, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: a lemma is a proposition proved as a step towards a theorem
L for learner, from the L-plates on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A girl provides a premise for a maths problem as a student breaks loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is a common female first name, so it stands for a girl.

clue.text: Denial is genuine, victim admitted

indicators.note: someone admitted to a place is let inside it

parts.note: real means genuine
the butt of a joke is its victim

explanation.surface: Someone insists their denial is true, with the victim allowed in.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebuttal is a contradiction or refutation of a claim, a form of denial.

clue.text: Weak little creature?

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for weak
an imp is a small mischievous sprite

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a feeble person is a weak creature, and the letters come from weak plus a small sprite.
explanation.definitionFit: A wimp is a feeble, timid person, which the whole clue describes playfully.

clue.text: Very small arachnid finally put on record

parts.note: minute, pronounced my-NEWT, means tiny

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is used

parts.note: the last letter of arachnid

explanation.surface: A tiny spider ends up recorded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very small arachnid' reads as one creature, perhaps a mite, but splits after its second word.
explanation.definitionFit: To minute something is to write it into the minutes, the official record of a meeting.

clue.text: Working for nothing, coming in so menacing-sounding

indicators.note: pieces coming into a word enter it and sit between its letters

parts.note: thus and so both mean in this way, or therefore
under, as of someone working under a boss
nought, the figure zero

explanation.surface: Someone unpaid moves in, and so sounds threatening.
explanation.walkthrough: The working word and the nought go between the first two and last two letters of the word for so.
explanation.definitionFit: Thunderous describes a loud, rumbling sound like thunder, the noise of an approaching storm or threat.

clue.text: Old American chap gets chucked out

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
US for the United States
Ted, a man's name, stands for any chap

explanation.surface: An elderly American man is thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: Ousted means expelled or forced out of a place or position, the same as thrown out.

clue.text: Sequence of characters starting aestheticism for goddess

wordplay.note: aestheticism opens with two characters in sequence: A, and after it E, spelt out as 'A, then E'

explanation.surface: A string of letters beginning an essay on aestheticism stands for a goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the letter sequence as a phrase: the first letter, then the word for 'next', then the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Athene, also spelt Athena, is the Greek goddess of wisdom.

clue.text: Very quickly on lovey-dovey terms when Dr. enters

indicators.note: what enters a word goes inside it, between its letters

parts.note: intime, a borrowing from French, means intimate and cosy
Dr. No, the villain of the first James Bond film

explanation.surface: A couple are quickly on affectionate terms once the doctor arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dr. needs its Bond villain surname; it goes after the first two letters of the cosy word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in no time is done almost at once, so the phrase means very quickly.

clue.text: Thin male coming out — that's after Giovanni's eaten superior food!

indicators.note: a person coming out leaves the place they were in, so that letter departs from the word

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for male
U means upper class or superior, as in U and non-U
è is Italian for 'is', so Giovanni's 'is' becomes E
slim means thin
surface padding for the Don Giovanni dinner picture

explanation.surface: A skinny man leaves, after Don Giovanni has eaten a fine meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The male letter comes out of the word for thin and leads the answer, with superior and the Italian 'is' between them; the parse is loose at best.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is a breakfast cereal of oats, nuts and dried fruit, so it is a food.

clue.text: I had warrant for taking time off — skiving?

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, so the letter for this unit is dropped

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I had
to warrant is to permit, to let

explanation.surface: Someone claims permission for a day off, but is really dodging work.
explanation.walkthrough: The scanned page lost the opening 'I'; time is T, removed from the end. Skiving is British slang for shirking work.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone skiving is avoiding work, so they are idle, doing nothing.

clue.text: He is so impetuous, but 'e isn't!

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a rash man is described as quick-tempered and reckless
setter's reading: the word 'He' has a head letter, but the cockney 'e has lost it

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the dropped-aitch 'e has had its head chopped off, the H, so it cannot be described by the answer's word for rash.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot-headed means impetuous and quick to anger, which describes the first He; the second has lost its head.

clue.text: The three here may sound very French

indicators.note: may sound means the word is heard as it is spoken, matching another word's pronunciation

parts.note: très is French for very

explanation.surface: Someone notes that the three people here might sound very French.
explanation.definitionFit: A trey is the three in a pack of cards or on a die.

clue.text: Theatre offers two sopranos flanking harmonica-player — excellent!

indicators.note: items flanking something stand on either side of it, so one goes before and one after

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for soprano, used twice
Larry Adler, the famous American harmonica virtuoso
swell is dated slang for excellent

explanation.surface: A theatre stages two sopranos either side of a harmonica player, and the show is superb.
explanation.walkthrough: The harmonica player and the slang word for excellent together sit between the two singers. Sadler's Wells is a famous London theatre for dance and opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadler's Wells is a long-established London theatre, so it is an example of the definition.
